podcast.title: Formation (1970)
podcast.body: The band was formed in Cleveland in 1970, initiating their influential run in the music scene. "They were formed in Cleveland in 1970."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation and Style (1970-1975)
podcast.body: The Razberries, a group from Cleveland, were active from 1970 to 1975. They produced songs with melodies reminiscent of the bubblegum pop side of British glam rock, but distinctively incorporated elements of the classic American garage band sound, which also foreshadowed the new wave music that emerged later in the decade. "They existed for five years, 1970 to 1975. And during that period, they released some killer songs with melodies that sort of ran parallel with the bubblegumny pop side of British glam rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Peak Years (1972-1974)
podcast.body: The band experienced their most successful period between 1972 and 1974, marked by significant hits and critical recognition. "Their best years were between 1972 and 1974."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Distinctive Sound
podcast.body: The Raspberries differentiated themselves through their unique combination of riff-heavy guitars and catchy pop melodies. "What made them different was their mating of riffig guitars and pop melodies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Wave American Powerpop
podcast.body: The Raspberries, fronted by Eric Carmen, were one of the primary American bands in the first wave of power pop. "first wave of Powerpop bands were mostly American, such as the Eric Carmen fronted The Raspberry."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Power Pop Pioneers
podcast.body: The Raspberries are widely regarded as a groundbreaking band in the Power Pop genre, with their name being synonymous with the sound. "Ask anyone about Power Pop, and they will talk about the raspberries."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recording Technique - Limiter Use
podcast.body: For their punchy mix, particularly on songs like "Go All the Way," the band utilized a prototype outboard device known as a limiter in 1972. This state-of-the-art equipment contributed an extra "oomph of power" to their sound. "It used a prototype outboard device called a limiter, state of the art stuff in 1972. And that gave everything an extra oomph of power."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sporadic Reunions
podcast.body: Following their initial run, The Raspberries had occasional reunions, bringing their music back to fans. "There were also sporadic reunions in the raspberries."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Precursors to Other Powerpop Bands
xref.body: Big Star predated other successful Powerpop bands of the 1970s, such as Badfinger, Todd Rundgren, The Raspberries, Cheap Trick, and The Knack, establishing the genre's foundation before its wider recognition. "There were other Powerpop bands in the 70s who had hits. There was Bad Finger and Todd Rungren. We had the raspberries, Cheap Trick, the Nack, but Big Star was there before all of them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

xref.title: Signature Gibson Melody Maker
xref.body: Joan Jett's primary guitar for many years was a white Gibson Melody Maker, which she acquired from Eric Carmen after The Raspberries disbanded. This guitar was famously used on The Raspberries' hit "Go All The Way" and is heard on many of Jett's own successful songs. She later collaborated with Gibson on her own signature Melody Maker models, released in 2008 and 2010. "For the longest time, Joan Jett's main guitar has been a white Gibson melody maker."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
